    <div class="content">
        <h2 id="overview"><i class="fas fa-bullseye"></i> 1. What is MITRE ATT&CK?</h2>

        <h3>Understanding the Basics</h3>
        <p>Imagine you're learning to defend a castle. You'd want to know:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>How do attackers typically get in? (scaling walls, breaking gates, bribery...)</li>
            <li>What do they do once inside? (search for treasure, take hostages, burn buildings...)</li>
            <li>How have past attackers operated? (specific techniques used by famous armies)</li>
        </ul>

        <p><strong>MITRE ATT&CK</strong> is exactly this - but for cyber attacks. It's a comprehensive "playbook" of
            how hackers actually attack organizations, based on real incidents that have been studied and documented
            over years.</p>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Think of it like this:</strong> If hackers were chess players,
            ATT&CK would be a book containing EVERY possible move they might make, organized by what they're trying
            to achieve. Instead of just knowing "hackers are bad," you know specifically: "Hackers often use
            PowerShell (T1059.001) to run commands because it's already installed on Windows computers."
        </div>

        <h3>The Technical Definition</h3>
        <p><strong>MITRE ATT&CK</strong> (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) is a
            globally-accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations.
            It serves as a common language for describing cyber attacks.</p>

        <p>The framework is maintained by MITRE, a nonprofit that operates federally funded R&D centers. They've
            catalogued thousands of attacks and distilled them into a structured framework anyone can use.</p>

        <h3>Why ATT&CK Changed Everything</h3>
        <p>Before ATT&CK, security teams had a problem. When analysts discussed attacks, they'd say things like:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>"The attacker ran some scripts"</li>
            <li>"They moved around the network"</li>
            <li>"They stole data somehow"</li>
        </ul>
        <p>This was vague and made it hard to compare attacks, build defenses, or communicate clearly.</p>

        <p>Now, with ATT&CK, those same descriptions become:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>"T1059.001 - PowerShell execution"</li>
            <li>"T1021.001 - Remote Desktop Protocol lateral movement"</li>
            <li>"T1048 - Exfiltration over alternative protocol"</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Real-World Example:</strong> When the Colonial Pipeline
            ransomware attack happened in 2021, security teams worldwide immediately shared analysis mapped to
            ATT&CK. Within hours, organizations could check: "Do we detect T1078 (Valid Accounts)? Do we detect
            T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact)?" This shared language accelerated global defense.
        </div>

        <h3>Key Use Cases</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Use Case</th>
                    <th>What It Means</th>
                    <th>Who Benefits</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Detection Engineering</strong></td>
                    <td>Build alerts that detect specific techniques</td>
                    <td>SOC Analysts, Security Engineers</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Threat Intelligence</strong></td>
                    <td>Describe threat actors by their TTPs instead of just IOCs</td>
                    <td>CTI Analysts, Threat Hunters</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Security Assessment</strong></td>
                    <td>Find gaps in your detection coverage</td>
                    <td>Security Managers, CISOs</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Red Teaming</strong></td>
                    <td>Structure adversary emulation tests</td>
                    <td>Penetration Testers, Red Teams</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Communication</strong></td>
                    <td>Speak the same language across teams and organizations</td>
                    <td>Everyone in security</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="structure"><i class="fas fa-sitemap"></i> 2. Framework Structure</h2>

        <h3>Understanding the Hierarchy (It's Like an Outline)</h3>
        <p>ATT&CK is organized like a well-structured document with increasing levels of detail:</p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Level</th>
                    <th>What It Is</th>
                    <th>Example</th>
                    <th>Count</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Matrices</strong></td>
                    <td>The environment (Windows/Mac/Linux, Mobile, Industrial)</td>
                    <td>Enterprise Matrix</td>
                    <td>3</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Tactics</strong></td>
                    <td>The adversary's GOAL (the "WHY")</td>
                    <td>Credential Access</td>
                    <td>14</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Techniques</strong></td>
                    <td>HOW they achieve the goal</td>
                    <td>OS Credential Dumping</td>
                    <td>~200</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Sub-techniques</strong></td>
                    <td>Specific variations of techniques</td>
                    <td>LSASS Memory</td>
                    <td>~400</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Procedures</strong></td>
                    <td>Exact implementation by specific threat actors</td>
                    <td>Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords</td>
                    <td>Thousands</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Walk-Through Example:</strong><br>
            <strong>Tactic:</strong> Credential Access (goal: steal credentials)<br>
            <strong>Technique:</strong> T1003 - OS Credential Dumping<br>
            <strong>Sub-technique:</strong> T1003.001 - LSASS Memory<br>
            <strong>Procedure:</strong> APT28 uses Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords command<br><br>
            <em>Translation: The attacker wanted passwords (tactic), so they dumped operating system credentials
                (technique), specifically from LSASS memory (sub-technique), using the exact Mimikatz command the
                notorious APT28 group uses (procedure).</em>
        </div>

        <h3>The Three Matrices</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Enterprise:</strong> Windows, macOS, Linux, Cloud (AWS/Azure/GCP), Network, Containers -
                this is the most commonly used matrix</li>
            <li><strong>Mobile:</strong> iOS and Android device attacks</li>
            <li><strong>ICS:</strong> Industrial Control Systems (power plants, manufacturing, SCADA)</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Common Beginner Mistake:</strong> Don't try to
            memorize all 200+ techniques! Start with the 10-15 most common techniques in your industry (check
            reports from CrowdStrike, Mandiant, or CISA). You'll naturally learn more as you encounter them in
            incidents.
        </div>

        <h2 id="tactics"><i class="fas fa-chess"></i> 3. The 14 Tactics Explained</h2>
        <p>Tactics represent the adversary's objective at each phase of an attack:</p>

        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0043: Reconnaissance</h4>
            <p>Gather information to plan attack</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0042: Resource Development</h4>
            <p>Establish attack infrastructure</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0001: Initial Access</h4>
            <p>Get into the network</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0002: Execution</h4>
            <p>Run malicious code</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0003: Persistence</h4>
            <p>Maintain foothold</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0004: Privilege Escalation</h4>
            <p>Gain higher permissions</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0005: Defense Evasion</h4>
            <p>Avoid detection</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0006: Credential Access</h4>
            <p>Steal credentials</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0007: Discovery</h4>
            <p>Learn the environment</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0008: Lateral Movement</h4>
            <p>Move through network</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0009: Collection</h4>
            <p>Gather target data</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0011: Command & Control</h4>
            <p>Communicate with implants</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0010: Exfiltration</h4>
            <p>Steal data out</p>
        </div>
        <div class="tactic-box">
            <h4>TA0040: Impact</h4>
            <p>Disrupt, destroy, manipulate</p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="techniques"><i class="fas fa-cogs"></i> 4. Understanding Techniques</h2>

        <h3>Technique Components</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Field</th>
                    <th>Description</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>ID</strong></td>
                    <td>Unique identifier (e.g., T1059)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Name</strong></td>
                    <td>Descriptive name (e.g., Command and Scripting Interpreter)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Description</strong></td>
                    <td>How the technique works</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Platforms</strong></td>
                    <td>Where it applies (Windows, Linux, macOS, etc.)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Data Sources</strong></td>
                    <td>Logs/telemetry for detection</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Detection</strong></td>
                    <td>Guidance on detecting the technique</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Mitigations</strong></td>
                    <td>How to prevent/reduce impact</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Most Common Techniques (2024-2025)</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><code>T1059</code> - Command and Scripting Interpreter (PowerShell, Python)</li>
            <li><code>T1078</code> - Valid Accounts (compromised credentials)</li>
            <li><code>T1566</code> - Phishing (spearphishing attachments/links)</li>
            <li><code>T1486</code> - Data Encrypted for Impact (ransomware)</li>
            <li><code>T1082</code> - System Information Discovery</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="mapping"><i class="fas fa-map"></i> 5. How to Map Threats</h2>

        <h3>Mapping Incident to ATT&CK</h3>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Extract Behaviors:</strong> What did the adversary DO? (not just what tools)</li>
            <li><strong>Identify Tactics:</strong> What was their goal at each step?</li>
            <li><strong>Match Techniques:</strong> Find the technique that describes the behavior</li>
            <li><strong>Document Evidence:</strong> Link to logs/artifacts that prove the technique</li>
        </ol>

        <h3>Example Mapping</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Observed Behavior</th>
                    <th>Tactic</th>
                    <th>Technique</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>User clicked phishing link</td>
                    <td>Initial Access</td>
                    <td>T1566.002 Spearphishing Link</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Macro executed PowerShell</td>
                    <td>Execution</td>
                    <td>T1059.001 PowerShell</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Added to registry Run key</td>
                    <td>Persistence</td>
                    <td>T1547.001 Registry Run Keys</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Dumped LSASS memory</td>
                    <td>Credential Access</td>
                    <td>T1003.001 LSASS Memory</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>RDP to other servers</td>
                    <td>Lateral Movement</td>
                    <td>T1021.001 Remote Desktop</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="detection"><i class="fas fa-eye"></i> 6. Detection Engineering</h2>

        <h3>Building ATT&CK-Based Detections</h3>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Choose Technique:</strong> Start with high-priority techniques based on threat landscape
            </li>
            <li><strong>Review Data Sources:</strong> What logs do you need?</li>
            <li><strong>Build Detection Logic:</strong> Create SIEM rule or query</li>
            <li><strong>Test with Emulation:</strong> Use Atomic Red Team or similar</li>
            <li><strong>Tune for Environment:</strong> Reduce false positives</li>
            <li><strong>Document Coverage:</strong> Map detection to technique ID</li>
        </ol>

        <h3>Example Detection (Splunk)</h3>
        <pre style="background: var(--bg-secondary); padding: 1rem; border-radius: 8px; overflow-x: auto;"><code># T1003.001 - LSASS Memory Access

index=sysmon EventCode=10 TargetImage=“*lsass.exe” | where NOT match(SourceImage, “(?i)(MsMpEng|csrss|wininit)”) | stats count by SourceImage, SourceUser, Computer | where count > 0

        <h2 id="coverage"><i class="fas fa-chart-pie"></i> 7. Coverage Analysis</h2>
        <p>Use ATT&CK to identify detection gaps:</p>

        <h3>Coverage Assessment Steps</h3>
        <ol>
            <li>Inventory all current detection rules</li>
            <li>Map each rule to ATT&CK technique(s)</li>
            <li>Visualize coverage using ATT&CK Navigator</li>
            <li>Identify gaps in critical tactics</li>
            <li>Prioritize based on threat intelligence</li>
        </ol>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Common Gaps:</strong> Organizations often have
            strong coverage for Initial Access and Execution, but poor coverage for Defense Evasion and Credential
            Access. Focus detection efforts on these blind spots.
        </div>

        <h2 id="navigator"><i class="fas fa-compass"></i> 8. ATT&CK Navigator</h2>
        <p>The ATT&CK Navigator is a web tool for visualizing and annotating the ATT&CK matrix.</p>

        <h3>Navigator Use Cases</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Visualize detection coverage (green = detected, red = gap)</li>
            <li>Compare threat actor TTPs to your defenses</li>
            <li>Plan red team operations</li>
            <li>Track remediation progress</li>
            <li>Create layers for different analysis views</li>
        </ul>

        <p><strong>Access Navigator:</strong> <a href="https://mitre-attack.github.io/attack-navigator/"
                target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">mitre-attack.github.io/attack-navigator</a></p>
